I am 58 and have farmed these 19.1 mu in Quzhou for 30 years. With only three mouths to feed at home, I need stable income without taking reckless risks. The wheat-maize rotation is my backbone—two crops a year on the same piece of land, prices are predictable, and I know the buyers. I will keep 15 mu in that rotation. The remaining 4.1 mu I will plant to cotton. Cotton demands more labor, especially for spraying, but the returns have been decent in recent years and it spreads my risk if grain prices dip.

For the wheat, I will sow an improved variety—something like Jimai 22 or Luyuan 502—around mid-October after a pass with the rotary tiller. I have well water, so I will irrigate four times: once before winter to help it settle, once when it turns green in spring, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I apply compound fertilizer as a basal dose and topdress with nitrogen at jointing. I have learned that four sprays—herbicide early, insecticide and fungicide as needed—keeps the field clean. A yield of about 900 jin per mu is what I reliably get.

For the summer maize, I plant a hybrid such as Denghai 605 right after the wheat harvest in early June. I see no reason to till again; no-tillage after wheat works fine here, saves diesel, and I do not lose yield. I apply compound fertilizer at sowing and irrigate twice—at jointing and at tasseling. Three or four pesticide applications cover weeds, borers, and leaf diseases. I expect around 1,000 jin per mu if the summer rains cooperate.

For the cotton, I rotary-till in late April and sow a hybrid variety. Cotton is picky about water and pests, so I irrigate three times through the season and spray roughly 18 times to control bollworms, aphids, and mites. I fertilize twice—basal compound at sowing and a topdressing when the plants start setting bolls. Seed cotton yields on my land run about 500 jin per mu.

I do not chase record yields. I manage for steady, profitable harvests using the inputs and practices that have worked for me for decades.
